title: How do you structure a case about making a process faster or cheaper?
description: "How can the client improve this process?" Operations cases: something is slow, costly or error-prone.
hook: Structure a process case by mapping the work from start to finish, finding the bottleneck (the slowest step, which caps the output of the whole process), and fixing that step first by eliminating, combining, re-ordering or simplifying work. Ask first which outcome matters most: cost, speed, capacity or quality. Then prove the bottleneck with simple capacity maths before recommending staff or machines.
body:
When you will use it

Use it when something is slow, costly or error-prone: a factory line that cannot keep up, a warehouse missing dispatch cut-offs, a clinic with long waits, a back office that takes weeks to approve a loan. It is a diagnose question: break the process into steps, find the one that holds everything up, then fix it. See which framework to use for each type of question for the other families.

Ask this first

Which outcome matters most here: cost, speed, capacity or quality? And what is off limits?

The answer changes the fix. Cutting cost might mean fewer people at a step; increasing capacity might mean more. If speed for the customer matters, you care about waiting time, not just how busy each machine is.

The structure

  • Map it
    • Steps and hand-offs
    • Time, cost and errors at each step
    • Where work queues up: the bottleneck
  • Fix the steps (often called ECRS)
    • Eliminate steps that add no value
    • Combine steps to cut hand-offs
    • Re-order steps so work runs in parallel
    • Simplify what remains, often with technology
  • Fix what supports them
    • People: skills, incentives, staffing by hour
    • Technology and systems

Make it your own

One principle drives the case: the slowest step sets the output of the whole process. Speeding up any other step adds nothing. So find the bottleneck, fix it, then ask which step becomes the new one.

Be precise about what you are measuring. Throughput is completed units per hour. Cycle time is how long one unit takes at a step. Lead time is how long the customer waits from request to completion. You can raise throughput and still leave customers waiting if arrivals bunch up at peak times, so name the outcome the client actually cares about.

A short worked example

An online retailer's warehouse misses its same-day dispatch cut-off on busy days. The figures are illustrative.

StageCapacity (orders per hour)
Picking120
Packing80
Dispatch100

Find the bottleneck. Packing caps the line at 80 orders an hour, even though picking and dispatch could handle more. Adding ten pickers would lift picking to 150 and change nothing.

Size the problem. At peak, 100 orders arrive an hour. Packing falls 20 an hour behind, so over a 10-hour peak 200 orders miss same-day dispatch. If each late order costs about $8 in refunds and upgraded shipping, that is $1,600 a day, or about $584k a year if it happens every day.

Fix it and check the next step. Two extra packing stations lift packing to 110 an hour. Output now rises to 100, because dispatch becomes the new bottleneck, which happens to match peak demand. If the stations cost $150k a year to run, they pay for themselves several times over. Before buying anything, though, try ECRS at the packing step: could pickers place items straight into shipping boxes (combine), or could standard box sizes cut packing time (simplify)?

Check the side effects. Measure error rates and damaged parcels as packing speeds up. A faster step that creates rework just moves the queue.

Strong and weak answers

A weak answer adds resources everywhere:

The warehouse should hire more staff and invest in automation to speed things up.

A strong answer follows the work and quantifies the constraint:

Packing handles 80 an hour against 100 arriving, so it is the bottleneck. More pickers would change nothing. Two packing stations would lift output to 100, and then dispatch becomes the limit.

The mistakes to avoid

  1. Speeding up a step that is not the bottleneck. It makes one team look busier and changes nothing for the customer.
  2. Adding people before simplifying. Remove or combine steps first; then add capacity where it is still short.
  3. Forgetting the next bottleneck. Every fix moves the constraint somewhere else.
  4. Running at 100% on paper. Real demand varies, so a step that matches average demand exactly will still build queues at peak.

Practise with real prompts

1. Quick maths: a clinic has 3 nurses doing 15-minute intakes and 2 doctors doing 20-minute consultations. Eight patients arrive an hour. Where is the bottleneck?

Show the answer

Intake capacity: 3 × 4 = 12 an hour. Doctor capacity: 2 × 3 = 6 an hour. Doctors are the bottleneck, and the queue grows by 2 patients an hour. A third doctor (9 an hour) fixes it; another nurse does nothing.

2. A parcel company's on-time delivery fell from 95% to 85%.

Show the answer
  • Where in the chain: collection, sorting hub, trunk transport between hubs, last mile.
  • Volume against capacity: parcel growth against vans, drivers and sorting hours; peaks by day and season.
  • Process and systems: route planning, scanning, missed hand-overs; any new system or hub?
  • External: weather, traffic, partner carriers, address problems.

Where to start: find the step where parcels start running late.

The trap: listing causes without locating where in the chain the delays start.

3. An airline's aircraft spend 20% longer on the ground between flights than rivals'.

Show the answer
  • Arrival: waiting for a gate, stand or tug; taxi times.
  • Aircraft servicing: cleaning, catering, fuel, bags.
  • Boarding: process, cabin bags, late passengers.
  • Planning: schedule buffers, crew connections, ground staff at peak.

Where to start: the critical path, the longest chain of steps that must happen one after another. Speeding up tasks off that chain does nothing.

The trap: trying to speed up every task.
